title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Data Revolution




Development is undergoing a data revolution
More data than ever: surveys, satellites, sensors, social media
We seem to think more data is useful for answering important questions
But what kinds of questions can data actually answer?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Three Types of Questions


Descriptive: What is happening?

How many people live in poverty?

Predictive: What is likely to happen?

Which households are at risk of food insecurity?

Causal: What would happen if we intervened?

Would a cash transfer reduce poverty?




Data can help answer all three, but each demands its own toolkit

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Each Question Needs Different Tools


Description: How do we summarize? → Summary statistics
Prediction: How do we generalize? → Models
Causation: How do we reason about “what if”? → ???




Today’s focus: What toolkit does causation require?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Summary Statistics


Central Tendency
Where is the middle?


Mean: \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} X_i\)
Median: middle value
Mode: most frequent



Spread
How dispersed are the data?


Variance: \(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})^2\)
Standard deviation: \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\)

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Correlation: A Summary Statistic


Correlation summarizes co-variation in a single number:
\[r_{XY} = \frac{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \sum_{i}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]


- Ranges from -1 to +1 - Measures linear association

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
What Does Correlation Mean?
More colloquially: what do we mean when say that X and Y are correlated?


They tend to move together
When X is high, Y tends to be high (or low)
There is a systematic association in observed data

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
What Correlation Is (and Isn’t)




Technically: A measure that summarizes (linearly) how two numeric variables move together
Conceptually: The basis of inductive evidence: generalizable patterns



When we say “X and Y are correlated,” we’re saying:
“Here is a regularity worth noting.”


But it does not explain why the pattern exists.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Correlation Tells Us…




Strength: How tightly X and Y move together (0 to ±1)
Direction: Positive (both rise) or negative (one rises, other falls)
Nothing about why they move together




The UFOs and kidnappings really are correlated in the data!

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Limits of Description
Correlation and summary statistics are powerful for description

But if we want to answer causal questions…
“Would a cash transfer reduce poverty?”


…we need a different toolkit entirely.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Causation
What does it mean to say that X causes Y?

How is it different from saying they are correlated?



Take a moment to think about this.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Common Intuitions About Causation


People often say:


“X leads to Y”
“X produces Y”
“X makes Y happen”




These feel intuitive. X as the source of a change in Y. But notice what they don’t tell us…

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Hidden Problem




How would we know X is the source of a change in Y instead of just correlated?
Causality describes an assumed relationship that we can never directly observe!
Causation is, in a sense, metaphysical!

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
A Very Old Problem


What do we mean by a cause?
How could we ever know that X really causes Y?



Philosophers like David Hume pointed out this is not obvious at all

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Why Causation is Not Observable


We never directly observe causation. We observe:


Events
Sequences
Regularities




You flip a switch. The light turns on.
You see the switch move. You see the light turn on. You don’t see causation itself, you cannot follow the causal process, you do not see the electrical current etc.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Repetition Doesn’t Solve It
Even if the switch always turns on the light:


You still only observe regularity
Not necessity
Not causation itself



All the data in the world look the same whether causation is really there or not.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Problem for Science
If causation is not directly observable:


Correlation alone cannot answer causal questions
Observed patterns admit multiple explanations



So how does science, interested in causes and consequences, proceed?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Same Data, Different Questions


People who take vitamins tend to live longer.


Descriptive: Do vitamin users live longer? ✓
Predictive: Can vitamin use help predict lifespan? ✓
Causal: Would people live longer if they started taking vitamins? 🤔




Only the last question is causal — and it’s the hardest to answer.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Core Difficulty
Causal questions require a comparison:

What actually happened vs. What would have happened otherwise


But we never observe both.
This is called THE FUNDAMENTAL PROBLEM OF CAUSAL INFERENCE

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
A Question to Ponder


We’ve established: Correlation ≠ Causation


But what about the reverse?
Does causation imply correlation?



Think about it…

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Does Causation Imply Correlation?




Conceptually, yes. If X truly causes Y, then changes in X should produce systematic changes in Y
If X causes Y, we should see them move together (correlation)
But: correlation can exist without causation (spurious relationships)




Causation → Correlation (usually)
Correlation ↛ Causation (never automatically)

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Two Key Moves
Rather than trying to observe causation directly, scientists made two practical moves:


Define causality as a comparison between TWO counterfactual states
Shift from individual causal effects to averages



Let’s unpack each move.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Neyman–Rubin Framework


Jerzy Neyman and Donald Rubin formalized this approach:


Causality is defined through potential outcomes
Each unit has two potential states — we only observe one
Causality is always relative (treated vs. what?)

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Potential Outcomes Notation


For each unit \(i\), define:


\(Y_i(1)\): outcome if unit \(i\) receives treatment
\(Y_i(0)\): outcome if unit \(i\) does not receive treatment




These are the two potential outcomes.
Every unit has both — but we can only ever see one.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Individual Causal Effect
DEFINE causality as the effect of the pill for patient \(i\):
\[TE_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\]


This is a definition — it tells us what we mean by a causal effect.
But can we calculate it?

title: Correlation and Causation
section: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
text:
The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
For any patient, we observe only one outcome:


If they took the pill → we see \(Y_i(1)\)
If they didn’t → we see \(Y_i(0)\)




We never see the same patient both taking and not taking the pill

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Factual vs. Counterfactual


Factual: What we observe

Patient took the pill and recovered

Counterfactual: What would have happened

Would they have recovered without the pill?




To measure causal effects, we need both.
But we can never observe the counterfactual.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Why This Problem is Fundamental


No amount of data in the world lets us see both states for one patient
Ana took the pill and recovered — but would she have recovered anyway?
We will never know.




The individual treatment effect \(TE_i\) is unknowable. So what do we do?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Workaround
We can’t know the pill’s effect on any one patient.

But what if we could estimate the average effect across many patients?


The solution: Compare groups, not individuals.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
Instead of asking: “Did the pill help Ana?”

Ask: “On average, does the pill help patients recover?”


\[ATE = \overline{Y(1)} - \overline{Y(0)}\]
Average recovery rate with pill minus average recovery rate without pill.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Key Insight




We use the no-pill group to approximate what would have happened to the pill group
Their outcomes stand in for the missing counterfactual
This only works if the groups are comparable — similar in all relevant ways




Causal inference is the craft of building credible comparisons between groups.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Why Causality Matters for Development


Understanding cause and effect is how we change things in the real world
Causal inference separates good evaluations from bad

Did this program actually reduce poverty?
Would this policy improve outcomes?

Without causal reasoning, we’re just guessing

title: Correlation and Causation
section: Many Tools to Build Credible Comparisons
text:
Many Tools to Build Credible Comparisons




Randomized experiments

Random assignment makes treatment unrelated to differences

Observational methods

Natural experiments, Difference-in-Differences, Matching
Try to approximate the logic of randomization





We’ll explore these throughout the course.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Three Toolkits





Question
Toolkit




Description
Summary statistics (mean, variance, correlation)


Prediction
Models (extrapolate patterns)


Causation
Counterfactual reasoning + averages





Each is valuable. Each has limits. Don’t use the wrong tool for the job.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Today’s Key Points




Different questions need different tools — causal questions ask “what if?”
Causality = comparing two states (treatment vs. no treatment)
Fundamental Problem: We can’t observe both states for one person
Solution: Compare groups — if treatment is unrelated to differences, groups are comparable on average
Causal inference = building credible comparisons

title: Correlation and Causation
section: Correlation (in the summary statistic sense) Tells Us…
text:
Correlation (in the summary statistic sense) Tells Us…


Strength: How tightly X and Y move together (0 to ±1)
Direction: Positive (both rise) or negative (one rises, other falls)
Nothing about why they move together




The UFOs and patents really are correlated in the data!

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Causation is Not Observable
We never directly observe causation. We observe events, sequences and regularities

Everyday, you hear your doorbell and Mexican food appears
Doorbells cause Mexican food to appear.
Everyday, you sacrifice a child to Huitzilopotchli and the sun rises
Sacrifices cause sunrises
Whenever you flip the lightswitch, light turns on
Moving plastic objects on the wall turn on the light

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
A Misleading Claim


A pharmaceutical company says:

“Patient took our pill. Patient got better. Therefore, the pill works.”



What’s wrong with this reasoning?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Why This is Wrong




We saw the patient with the pill → got better
We didn’t see the patient without the pill
Maybe they would have gotten better anyway!




To know if the pill caused recovery, we need to compare two states of the world.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Causality is a Comparison


The causal question: Did the pill make the patient better?


To answer this, we need to compare:

What happened with the pill
What would have happened without the pill




Causality is always relative — treatment vs. what alternative?

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Defining the Key Terms




Units: The people (or things) we’re studying

Example: Patients who could take the pill

Treatment: A well-defined intervention we want to evaluate (more on this later)

Example: Taking the pill (vs. not taking it)

Outcome: What we measure

Example: Whether the patient recovered

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Potential Outcomes
For each patient, define two possible states of the world:


\(Y_i(1)\): What happens if patient \(i\) takes the pill
\(Y_i(0)\): What happens if patient \(i\) doesn’t take the pill



Every patient has both. But we can only ever see one.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
Why Do Averages Work?


People are different — Ana and Diana aren’t identical.


So how can comparing group averages tell us anything causal?



We need to make an assumption.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Logic of Comparison




Ana took the pill → recovered
Diana is just like Ana but didn’t take the pill → also recovered
Maybe the pill didn’t help Ana after all!




If we can find a statistical twin for every treated person, we can estimate causal effects.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
The Key Assumption


Assumption: The two groups are comparable on average.


This means: who takes the pill is unrelated to who would recover anyway.



If this assumption holds → group averages are valid comparisons → we can estimate causal effects.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
When Does This Hold?




Ana is sicker than Diana? Doesn’t matter — if sickness didn’t determine who got the pill
Some people recover faster? Doesn’t matter — if that’s unrelated to who got treatment
Individual differences cancel out when treatment is independent of those differences




Causal inference is the craft of making this assumption credible.

title: Correlation and Causation
text:
A Note on Definitions


There are many ways to define causality:


Legal: “But for” the defendant’s action, would harm have occurred?
Philosophical: Necessary and sufficient conditions, mechanisms
Social science: Counterfactual comparison (what we’ll use)




We focus on the social science approach — but know that others exist.
